extracted.intended_audience: education institution administrators, Title IX coordinators, legal counsel, and policy implementers
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble guidance and final-regulation definitions for Title IX (34 CFR part 106) clarifying how terms like domestic violence, stalking, relevant, remedies, respondent, student, recipient, program or activity, federal financial assistance, employee, and student with a disability should be interpreted and applied by recipients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "Domestic Violence"
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department adopts a definition of domestic violence that tracks VAWA 2022 language but omits the portion beginning with "in the case of victim services," and removes the modifying words "of violence" from "felony and misdemeanor crimes," to align more closely with VAWA 2022 while excluding language about VAWA-funded "victim services."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explains it was not legally obligated to incorporate the entire VAWA 2022 definition (including the victim‑services portion) into Title IX because "victim services" under VAWA refers to services not available under Title IX and VAWA definitions apply to grant programs. Omitting that language is not a substantive change for Title IX purposes and does not mean conduct described there cannot form the basis of sex‑based harassment findings. The Department kept reference to crimes (but removed "of violence") to track VAWA 2022 where relevant, and notes that coercive or controlling behavior that does not meet the domestic violence definition may nonetheless constitute sex‑based harassment if it meets elements of hostile‑environment harassment or other defined offenses. Recipients may comply with these regulations' definition and, to the extent applicable, other federal agency definitions (e.g., HUD). The Department declined to replace the proposed definitions with cross‑references to the Clery Act or VAWA 2022 because stakeholders found cross‑references confusing and direct statutory language is clearer. The Department also stated that recipients or Title IX implementers may rely on knowledge of jurisdictional criminal laws (as with Clery Act duties) and may include relevant crimes/definitions in training required under § 106.8(d)(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "Stalking"
rubrics_metrics.description: Stalking is defined (consistent with VAWA 2022 and 34 U.S.C. 12291(a)(36)) as a course of conduct directed at a specific person that would cause a reasonable person to fear for their safety or the safety of others or to suffer substantial emotional distress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department retained the 2020 amendments' stalking definition and declined to provide regulatory examples of elements, though it discussed terms. Key interpretive points: (1) a "course of conduct" requires more than one incident and must be directed at a specific person; (2) stalking can be in person or use technology, and duration, frequency, and intensity matter; (3) stalking tactics include (but are not limited to) watching, following, tracking devices, monitoring online activity, unwanted contact, property invasion/damage, hacking accounts, threats, sabotage, and attacks; (4) the "reasonable person" standard is interpreted as a reasonable person in the complainant's position (consistent with Clery Act definitions); (5) "substantial emotional distress" need not require medical or professional treatment or counseling to be shown; (6) the Department declined to adopt further definitional refinements (e.g., "menacing or invasive") and rejected vagueness/overbreadth concerns, citing case law (Rowles) upholding a similar standard; (7) recipients must consider disability and cultural context by applying the reasonable‑person-in-the-complainant's-position standard and must comply with disability and other nondiscrimination obligations (Section 504, ADA, Title VI); (8) for elementary/secondary students with disabilities, Title IX Coordinator should consult IEP or placement decision personnel as appropriate per § 106.8(e). Changes: None.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "Relevant"
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department retains a definition of "relevant" that allows inclusion of all evidence that is related to an allegation of sex discrimination and that may aid the decisionmaker in determining whether the alleged sex discrimination occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final definition is intended to assist recipients that lack substantial legal experience and reflects plain meaning rather than adopting Rule 401 of the Federal Rules of Evidence. The Department rejected narrowing "relevant" to only evidence that "may aid a decisionmaker" to the point of excluding related evidence; instead the two‑step explanation is: evidence/questions must first be related to the allegations under investigation, and if that threshold is met, then (a) questions are relevant when they seek evidence that may aid in showing whether the alleged sex discrimination occurred, and (b) evidence is relevant when it may aid a decisionmaker in determining whether alleged sex discrimination occurred. The Department will not provide concrete examples due to fact‑specificity, but it allows recipients to exclude questions/evidence that are related but would not aid a decisionmaker. The Department declined to: adopt the Federal Rules' definition, change the word "evidence" to "information," automatically consider all credibility‑related evidence relevant, or maintain the previous regulatory distinction between "directly related" evidence and "relevant" evidence. The regulations do not require adoption of a specific set of evidentiary rules; recipients may tailor procedures to their needs while following the prescribed balance for consistent grievance processes. The Department also reaffirmed access requirements in § 106.46(e)(6) and § 106.46 concerning investigatory reports and access to relevant, not otherwise impermissible evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "Remedies"
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedies are defined consistently with the 2020 amendments as individualized measures designed to restore or preserve access to the recipient's education program or activity for a particular complainant or other person or group of persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declined to produce a categorical list of what a remedy must look like because remedies are fact‑specific and individualized. It provided a non‑exhaustive list of possible measures that may be appropriate, such as: campus escorts; changes to class schedules or extracurriculars to separate complainant and respondent; adjustments to student housing; medical support and counseling; academic resources/support; review and potential correction of disciplinary actions if causally connected to harassment; reimbursement for counseling services; tuition adjustments; and any other remedies deemed appropriate. The Department rejected suggested language intended to constrain who may receive remedies (finding existing § 106.45(h)(3) and (4) adequate to prevent misuse) and clarified that remedies may be provided to complainants or others identified by the recipient as having had equal access limited or denied by sex discrimination, while disciplinary sanctions may be imposed on respondents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "Respondent"
rubrics_metrics.description: A "respondent" is a person in their individual capacity alleged to have engaged in conduct that could constitute sex discrimination under Title IX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department retained the 2020 preamble position that only individuals (not groups or organizations) can be respondents in Title IX grievance procedures. Recipients are not required to apply Title IX grievance procedures to groups or organizations but may address organizational misconduct through other applicable codes of conduct. The Department declined to change the definition to include entities, and noted that including volunteers as possible respondents may have recruitment consequences but that protecting civil rights justifies such coverage. Changes: None.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "Student With a Disability"
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulations include a definition of "student with a disability" to clarify the intersection of Title IX obligations with obligations to protect rights of students with disabilities and to define the scope of §§ 106.8(e) and 106.44(g)(6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department retained the definition despite comments arguing it was unnecessary because Title IX applies to all students. It declined to add an ADA cross‑reference (redundant) or to substitute alternative labels (e.g., "disabled student"), preferring the familiar phrase "student with a disability." The Department declined to adjudicate particular applications to specific populations, noting such determinations are fact‑specific. Changes: None.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "Title IX"
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department revised the definition of "Title IX" in the regulations to add 20 U.S.C. 1689 (which codified the interagency task force on sexual violence in education created by the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2022).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change reflects statutory direction in Public Law 117‑103 and ensures the list of sections that comprise Title IX in the regulatory definition is current. Changes: added section 1689 to the list of sections in title 20 that comprise Title IX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "Employee"
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declined to add a uniform regulatory definition of "employee," leaving recipients responsible for determining who is an employee for reporting and training obligations under § 106.44(c) and § 106.8(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because employment arrangements vary across recipients and State law, the Department determined recipients are best positioned to define who qualifies as an employee for institution‑specific reporting and training obligations. The preamble directs readers to discussion in related sections (§ 106.44(c) and § 106.8(d)) for further context. Changes: None.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "Federal Financial Assistance"
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declined to amend the definition of "Federal financial assistance" despite comments prompted by court decisions about tax‑exempt status; the Department's current position is that typical tax benefits/exemptions/deductions are not included in statutory/regulatory definitions of Federal financial assistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department noted authorities (e.g., 42 U.S.C. 2000d‑1; 28 CFR 42.102(c); 31 CFR 28.105; 34 CFR 106.2(g)) and court decisions indicating most tax benefits are not contractual federal assistance, and thus generally are not Federal financial assistance. The Department also observed that its Title IX regulations only apply to recipients who receive funds from the Department, so whether a given institution may be a recipient for other purposes is outside the scope of these regulations. Changes: None.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "Program or Activity"
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department retained the existing regulatory definition of "program or activity" consistent with statutory meaning and the Civil Rights Restoration Act of 1987, declining to narrow it to only programs/activities related to elementary, secondary, or postsecondary education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explained that because Title IX prohibits discrimination in a recipient's "education program or activity," a fact‑specific inquiry is required to determine whether a particular program or activity of a non‑educational institution is "educational" and covered. The Department reiterated precedent that if any part of an educational institution receives federal funds, all its operations are covered by Title IX (citing case law). Changes: None.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "Recipient"
rubrics_metrics.description: The longstanding regulatory definition of "recipient" (entities that receive federal assistance directly or through an intermediary) remains in effect and applies to charter school operating companies and subcontractors that receive Federal financial assistance through intermediaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responding to comments and the Fourth Circuit's Peltier decision, the Department agreed that entities receiving funds directly or through an intermediary are recipients within the meaning of Title IX, and therefore declined to amend the definition. The preamble cites Supreme Court precedent and Peltier to explain that charter school operators and subcontractors who receive federal assistance directly or through an intermediary fall within the definition. Changes: None.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "Student"
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department retains the longstanding definition of "student" as a person who has gained admission to an educational institution (a definition in effect since 1975), which includes applicants for admission and admitted students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department acknowledged comments that the definition may be overly broad (including persons admitted but not enrolled) or too narrow (not covering dual‑enrollment students, auditors, or sporadic enrollees). It declined to change the definition, noting the historical practice since HEW's 1975 regulations and that recipients have long been required to notify students (including persons who have gained admission) of nondiscrimination policies and to resolve complaints. The Department emphasized Title IX protects applicants and admitted students and that appropriate access to policies/procedures is required for those persons. Changes: None.
